newsitem.title: GREECE: No knock-out punch in Greek election TV duel.
newsitem.headline: No knock-out punch in Greek election TV duel.

text.p: Greece's technocrat Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis and his outspoken challenger Miltiades Evert locked horns in a television debate on Friday but no clear winner emerged from the duel.

With national elections only nine days away, the two rival camps had hoped the first such debate in Greece would tip the scales in the close race but no knock-out punches were delivered and the two candidates seemed locked in dead heat.
"Evert appeared energetic, personable and direct while Simitis expressed his views clearly and focused on the future," a television analyst said.
The demure Simitis, 60, kept his cool and stood by his views despite repeated attacks by the stocky Evert, 57, who picked on the premier's handling of a crisis with Turkey in January.
The two NATO members almost went to war over an uninhabited islet in the eastern Aegean. The crisis was averted with U.S. intervention after Greece removed its flag from the Imia islet.
Simitis, who was accused of rushing to compromise on the dispute, said that his cool-headed handling averted war.
"Has the Greek army left Imia and can it return there tomorrow?" the conservative party leader asked.
Simitis cooly responded: "If I had to handle the issue again, I would handle it the same way."
An informal private TV Skai channel call-in poll showed 11,250 people preferred Simitis to Evert, who got 10,197 calls.
Analysts said Evert appeared concerned about the average Greek and offered immediate solutions to his problems, such as selling state companies to boost development and create jobs.

"They are two leaders with different styles -- one is professorial, cool while Evert is more spontaneous. I would have called it a draw but there was such a high expectation on Simitis and such a low one on Evert that I would say he (Evert) won," said political analyst Costas Arvanitopoulos.
Public opinion polls show the two main contenders are running neck-and-neck while the Greek public remains unusually apathetic to the election.
Simitis, who called the snap election confident he was leading the polls, has seen the conservatives rise dangerously close as election day approaches.

The TV debate signalled a change in election style by the new generation of Greek politicians, who have opted for media-oriented campaigns rather than the traditional balcony speeches of their predecessors.
But with polls showing Greeks unimpressed by the characters and issues of the race, analysts say the modern campaign styles may have failed to inspire voters.

Past Greek elections have been dominated by flamboyant figures such as late socialist leader Andreas Papandreou and conservative party founder Constantine Karamanlis, who delighted in delivering rousing speeches before huge crowds.
Simitis, who succeeded Papandreou in January, bears little resemblance to his maverick mentor, shying away from populist rhetoric and focusing on European Union targets.
With both the main parties offering less than glamorous leaders, voters seem to be turning more than ever towards smaller parties, which have a surprisingly strong showing in opinion polls.
